title: Why Your Team Photos Make or Break Your Company Image
summary: Team photos are one of the first things visitors check. Here's what inconsistent, low-resolution or off-brand photos cost you, and how to plan a shoot that fixes it.
body_markdown:
## Key Takeaways


- **Inconsistent team photos read as disorganization.** Visitors register it before they can explain why.
- **Low-resolution photos cost you coverage.** Journalists pull images straight from your About page.
- **Google's guidance asks whether it is clear who created your content.** Named faces are part of how a company answers that.
- **Employee-supplied photos optimize for personal preference,** not for how the team page holds together.
- **One photographer, one session, one setup** is what makes a team page look deliberate rather than assembled.


Your team photos do more work than most companies give them credit for. The About Us page is one of the first places a customer, investor or journalist clicks, and the faces on it turn a company from a logo into people worth dealing with. Most businesses still treat that page as an afterthought and fill it with whatever headshots employees happen to own. Here is what that costs.


*One background, one lighting setup. Repeat it and the whole page looks deliberate.*


## Inconsistent Team Photos


Are your team photos the same size and crop? Do they share a background, a lighting style and a level of formality? Inconsistent photos are not merely untidy. They present an image of disorganization, and visitors register it before they could explain what is wrong.


‍


Look at two or three competitors' team pages, because that is the comparison a prospect is making. Consistency separates a page that looks considered from one assembled out of a shared drive. Running it as[a corporate headshot program](https://www.snappr.com/blog/corporate-headshots) rather than a one-off is what holds that together as the team changes.


## Low-Resolution Photos


Your About Us section is where writers go for images when you have no published press kit. Their universal requirement is high resolution, and a grainy 400-pixel crop lifted from a phone gives a journalist a reason to run the story without your photo, or without your company at all.


‍


It is also the page people use to decide whether to trust you.[Usability research on About Us content](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/about-us-information-on-websites/) found that the organizations which stood out used realistic photography of actual employees rather than stock images, and that readers expect authenticity there above all.


‍


Shoot and store at full resolution even if the site only ever serves a small version. Having it and not needing it costs nothing. Needing it on a deadline and not having it costs you the placement.


## Off-Brand Team Photos


Decide what impression you want the page to leave, then check whether the photos deliver it. If you are a casual company, rigid studio headshots against a gray backdrop say the opposite. If you are selling precision, an array of shots clearly taken on somebody's phone undermines every other claim on the site.


‍


The effect is measurable rather than cosmetic, and[professional headshots build trust](https://www.snappr.com/blog/how-professional-headshots-build-trust-and-increase-brand-credibility-by-78) in ways an inconsistent grid never will.


## Employee-Provided Photos


Asking everyone to send in a photo feels efficient and produces the worst version of this page. People choose on personal preference: a flattering holiday snap, a cropped wedding photo, a picture they simply like. None of those criteria have anything to do with whether the page holds together.


‍


The result is a grid of different resolutions, backgrounds and moods. Even when every individual photo is fine, the set is not, and the set is what visitors see.


## No Professional Touch


Most people dislike being photographed, and it shows. Left to a colleague with a phone, the usual outcome is a row of stiff, self-conscious faces.


‍


Getting someone to relax in front of a camera is a skill, and it is most of what you are paying a professional for. People come to your team page to connect with the humans behind the company, and genuine beats formal every time.


## What Google Sees on Your About Us Page


This part did not exist when most team pages were built. Google's[guidance on helpful content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks a blunt question: is it self-evident to your visitors who authored your content? It goes on to say that what helps people understand a page's experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trustworthiness is when it is clear who created it, and that of those four, trust matters most.


‍


A team page with real names, roles and faces is one of the plainest ways a company answers that question. It is not a ranking trick and nobody should treat it as one. It is evidence that identifiable people stand behind the business.


*Shooting in your own space costs nothing extra and dates far more slowly than a studio backdrop.*


## Planning Team Photos That Work


Book one photographer for one session and shoot everyone in the same place, in the same light, against the same background. That single decision solves consistency, resolution and brand fit at once.


‍


Brief the photographer on the impression you want rather than leaving it to be guessed, and agree the crop and framing in advance so every portrait matches. Then plan for the thing that breaks every team page eventually: new starters. Book a short top-up session each quarter, or agree a setup the photographer can reproduce months later, and the page stays coherent instead of drifting back into a patchwork.


## When to Bring In a Professional


If your team sits in one office and you need a dozen portraits, this is a half-day job that will outlast three website redesigns. Spread across cities, the harder problem is consistency between locations rather than the photography.

‍
